sharedText: every man his wife and his children
reason: The chapter's top-ranked machine candidate and a five-word run, and the senses are opposed. In 1 Samuel 30:22 the men of Belial propose that the two hundred who did not fight be given back their wives and children and nothing else — the clause is a formula of exclusion from spoil, spoken by the worst men in David's company and immediately overruled by him. In 3 Nephi 19:1 it describes an orderly, blessed dispersal after Christ's ascension. Nothing else of the verse is present, and taking one's own household home is not a distinctive act needing a source.

Recorded because a reader who knows the Fourth Gospel will propose it and should be told the catalogue saw it. John 7:53 — “And every man went unto his own house” — is the KJV's one verse of that shape, and its setting is a genuine parallel: a multitude divided about Jesus disperses, and the very next clause has Jesus going up the mount of Olives. 3 Nephi 19:1 has Jesus ascending into heaven and the multitude dispersing to their homes. But the wording will not carry it. The Book of Mormon reads “did return to his own home”, and “his own home” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 19:27, the beloved disciple taking Mary away from the cross — which is a different verse, a different phrase and an unrelated sense. What is actually shared with John 7:53 is “every man” and the idea of going home, and the register at 1 Nephi 1:5 covers connective matter of that weight.

sharedText: the Father in the name of
reason: A six-word run and the highest-scoring candidate at 19:6 and 19:8, and it is the Book of Mormon's own liturgical formula rather than a borrowing. “Pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus” occurs four times in this chapter alone (19:6, 19:7, 19:8, and the pattern behind 19:9) and has been the prescribed form since 3 Nephi 18:19-21, where Christ commands it. Ephesians 5:20 is about giving thanks always for all things, and shares no content word beyond the two nouns the formula requires. This entry covers every “Father in the name of” candidate in the chapter.

The n-gram stream ranked Isaiah 11:16 because it contains “came up out of the”; its next word is “land”, and the sentence is about Israel's highway from Assyria in the day it came up out of the land of Egypt. The Book of Mormon's next word is “water”. The borrowing at this verse is catalogued to Acts 8:39, where “come up out of the water” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. A model instance of the window closing one word early (ADJUDICATING §4).

“Angels came and ministered unto him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:11, the close of the temptation in the wilderness, and 3 Nephi 19:14 reads “angels did come down out of heaven, and did minister unto them”. The rarity is misleading: the shorter “ministered unto him” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and covers servants, women and the myriads of Daniel 7:10, so what is rare is only the collocation with “angels”, which the King James Bible has just twice (Matthew 4:11 and Mark 1:13, of the same episode). Against that, the Book of Mormon has already used this exact sentence eighteen verses earlier — 3 Nephi 17:24, “they were encircled about with fire; and the angels did minister unto them” — so 19:14 is the narrator repeating his own clause from the same visit, not reaching for Matthew. The 1830's “do bear record” (1920: “did bear record”) is preserved for the same reason it matters at 19:33: the present tense is the writer's, not a source's.

sharedText: and commanded them that they should
reason: A six-word run of pure command-report syntax. Mark 6:8's object is a staff, no scrip, no bread and no money for the mission of the twelve; 3 Nephi 19:16's is kneeling down on the earth. The same standing exclusion covers Matthew 16:20 at 19:17 (“his disciples that they should”), where Matthew's object is telling no man that he was the Christ.

sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is entirely the “and it came to pass” formula plus a temporal subordinator. The standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers it; it is named here only because nine words invites a second look. Amos 7:2 concerns the locusts finishing the grass of the land. The same applies to Mark 2:23 at 19:31.

The best-looking machine proposal in the chapter and it must be discharged carefully, because “bowed himself to the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bowed himself to the earth” occurs in none — so the Book of Mormon's clause is closer to Genesis 33:3 than to anything else in the King James Bible. It is still not the source. Genesis 33:3 is Jacob approaching Esau, bowing seven times in fear of a brother he has cheated; there is no prayer in it, no withdrawal, and no second party. The link at this verse is to Matthew 26:39 and its sequel, on the strength of the chapter's reproduction of Gethsemane's whole six-movement structure at 19:19, 19:24, 19:27, 19:30, 19:31 and 19:35 — where the posture clause stands in the slot Matthew fills with “fell on his face” and Mark with “fell on the ground”. The Book of Mormon's substitution of “the earth” for either is what produced the Genesis match, and it is a substitution, not a citation.

Five words of petitionary boilerplate. Acts 24:4 is Tertullus flattering Felix — “that I be not further tedious unto thee, I pray thee that thou wouldest hear us of thy clemency a few words” — where “I pray thee” is the ordinary courtesy of address, not prayer at all. 3 Nephi 19:21 is Christ petitioning the Father for the Holy Ghost. The idiom is common to both because English uses one verb for both senses.

Four words in a chapter that says “pray unto” eleven times. 2 Chronicles 6:34 is Solomon's dedicatory prayer asking that Israel's prayers toward the temple be heard when the army goes out to war; the shared material is a verb, a preposition and a pronoun. Worth naming only because 19:22 is doctrinally the most exposed verse in the chapter — “they pray unto me because I am with them” — and a reader may expect a source behind it. The catalogue finds none; the argument the verse is making is answered from John 20:28 at 19:18, not from Chronicles.

Four words of narrative pointing, and the verse's top-ranked candidate only because the surrounding phrase “upon them and behold they were” is uncommon. Genesis 40:6 is Joseph finding Pharaoh's butler and baker sad in the morning. The real borrowings at 19:25 are catalogued to Numbers 6:24-26 and Mark 9:3.

A five-word run, and Isaiah 60:21 does end “the work of my hands, that I may be glorified”. But the Book of Mormon's clause is “that I may be glorified in them”, and “I am glorified in them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 17:10, four verses from the John 17:9 sentence that 3 Nephi 19:29 reproduces for thirteen consecutive words. The prepositional phrase Isaiah lacks is exactly the phrase that decides it. Registered here so that a reader following the n-gram scores is sent to the link at this verse.
